meta.source: Team documents 'Analog limits: Earth - Mars' and 'Analog limits: Earth - Moon (south pole)'
meta.note: Many numbers are marked 'to be verified' in the source documents. Radiation, pressure and gravity are deliberately excluded from the similarity metric.
meta.criteria_link_note: The 'criteria' field links a mitigation to similarity criteria (s_*) for the site panel. This mapping was added by the team; it is not stated in the source documents.

mars.summary: Earth analogs are suitable for field geology, drilling, cold operations, prospecting for ice and salts, and studying dry soils. They do not replace testing in a thin CO2 atmosphere, under space radiation and at Martian gravity.

factors.name: Atmosphere and pressure
factors.why: Wind moves sand differently, liquid water is unstable on the surface, equipment and materials behave differently.

factors.name: Radiation
factors.target: No global magnetic field or ozone layer; surface dose about 0.6-0.7 mSv/day (Curiosity RAD, to be verified)
factors.earth: ~2.4 mSv/year on average from natural sources
factors.why: Requires shelters and limited working time; cannot be tested on Earth.

factors.name: Gravity
factors.why: Changes the behaviour of soil, drilling, walking and loads.

factors.name: Temperature
factors.target: Much colder than Earth, daily range of tens of degrees; in polar winter the surface reaches the CO2 frost point (about -125 C)
factors.earth: Coldest places on Earth about -90 C
factors.why: Earth has no long-lasting cold of this kind combined with a thin atmosphere.

factors.name: Ultraviolet
factors.target: Hard UV reaches the surface, no ozone layer
factors.why: Destroys organics on the surface; Earth deserts do not reproduce this.

factors.name: Regolith
factors.target: Fine iron-rich dust and sand; contains perchlorates (~0.5 wt% at the Phoenix site, to be verified); oxidizing and toxic
factors.earth: Soils altered by water, wind and organisms
factors.why: Perchlorates are hazardous to equipment and people; Earth soils do not mimic this.

factors.name: Water and ice
factors.target: Ground ice in the northern plains, hydrated minerals, traces of ancient lakes
factors.why: Earth analogs have biological processes and seasonal liquid water that Mars lacks today.

factors.name: Day and seasons
factors.target: Sol ~24 h 40 min, year 687 Earth days, axial tilt 25.19 deg
factors.earth: Day 24 h, year 365 days, tilt 23.44 deg
factors.why: A good match, but the long seasons differ.

factors.name: Dust storms
factors.target: Global storms can block the Sun for weeks
factors.why: They change temperature and power supply; Earth has no full analog.

mitigations.method: Low-pressure CO2 chambers combined with Martian soil simulants such as JSC Mars-1A.
Laboratory UV and irradiation sources, since Earth conditions do not reproduce them.
Parabolic flights, offloading suspension rigs, water immersion.
Laboratory tests with perchlorates at safe concentrations; soil simulants such as JSC Mars-1A.
Closed missions such as the Mars Desert Research Station (MDRS) to test crew work and procedures.
Drilling in McMurdo permafrost as a rehearsal for work in the Martian northern plains.

good_at: Cold and aridity: McMurdo Dry Valleys give realistic hyperarid cold-desert conditions for testing equipment and sampling methods.
Dry permafrost and salts: McMurdo and Don Juan Pond allow study of soils with perchlorates and brines.
Impact structures in desert: Roter Kamm shows how wind and sand modify a crater over time.
Dunes and wind erosion: Namibia provides material for studying dune shapes and motion.
Day length: the Martian sol nearly matches the Earth day, so rover and crew schedules can be rehearsed in real time.
mars.conclusion: The similarity ranking shows which Earth site is closest to a Martian reference in temperature, relief, ice, composition and illumination. It does not claim the site fully reproduces Mars. Pressure, radiation and gravity need dedicated test stands and chambers.

moon.summary: Earth analogs are suitable for rehearsing logistics, drilling, cold operations, ice prospecting and studying impact rocks. They do not replace testing in vacuum, under space radiation and at lunar gravity.

factors.name: Atmosphere and pressure
factors.why: No wind, fog, scattered light or heat exchange through air; equipment and materials behave differently.

factors.name: Radiation
factors.target: Direct galactic cosmic rays and solar flares; measured dose about 1.4 mSv/day (Chang'E-4)
factors.why: Requires shelters and limited working time; cannot be tested on Earth.

factors.name: Gravity
factors.why: Changes the behaviour of soil, drilling, walking, loads and dust.

factors.name: Permanently shadowed regions
factors.target: Crater cold traps without sunlight for billions of years; temperature can drop to -230 C and below
factors.earth: Coldest places on Earth about -90 C
factors.why: Earth has nothing close to the conditions in which the ice is preserved.

factors.name: Polar illumination
factors.target: Sun stays within about +/-1.5 deg of the horizon (lunar axial tilt 1.54 deg)
factors.earth: In polar regions the Sun rises to 30-40 deg; polar night in winter
factors.why: Long shadows and sharp contrast on the Moon are of a completely different nature.

factors.name: Regolith
factors.target: Sharp glassy dust formed by micrometeorite impacts, electrostatically charged
factors.earth: Soils altered by water, wind and organisms
factors.why: Dust damages mechanisms and breathing systems; Earth soil does not mimic this.

factors.name: Day cycle
factors.target: One lunar day lasts ~29.5 Earth days
factors.why: Changes thermal regime, power supply and work schedule.

factors.name: Water and life
factors.target: Water as ice in the soil (LCROSS: about 5.6 wt% at Cabeus); no life
factors.why: Earth analogs bring contamination and biological processes absent on the Moon.

mitigations.method: Thermal-vacuum chambers with regolith simulants (for example the anorthosite-based highlands simulant LHS-1).
Highlands regolith simulant LHS-1, based on anorthosite.
High altitude lowers pressure only partly and raises cosmic-ray dose only moderately: a supplement, not a replacement.
Mechanical suspension and offloading systems, parabolic flights, water immersion.
Closed missions at stations such as the Haughton-Mars Project to test crew psychology, resources and procedures in critical situations.
Rehearsing ice extraction from permafrost on Devon and Ellesmere islands as a step toward lunar craters.

good_at: Impact structures in the right rocks: Mistastin shows how an impact alters anorthosite; Haughton helps study crater morphology and expedition logistics.
Cold and permafrost: Devon and Ellesmere give realistic conditions for equipment and people at low temperatures.
Ground ice: Fosheim and permafrost valleys allow testing of drilling, radar sounding and ice extraction.
Illumination geometry with long shadows on a polar plateau, although the Sun is higher than on the Moon.
moon.conclusion: The similarity ranking shows which Earth site is closest to a lunar reference in temperature, relief, ice, composition and illumination. It does not claim the site fully reproduces the Moon. Vacuum, radiation and gravity need dedicated test stands and chambers.

unmapped_criteria.craters: No mitigation in the source documents.

unmapped_criteria.sun: No mitigation in the source documents; the low polar Sun cannot be reproduced on Earth.
